description: Achaleshwar Mahadev Temple lies just outside Achalgarh fort in Abu Road tehsil, Sirohi district, a few kilometres from Mount Abu. It is dedicated to Shiva as Achaleshwar, 'the immovable lord'. Instead of a conventional carved image, the sanctum has a natural stone form; local tradition holds that the shrine was built around the toe or footprint of Shiva, and a hollow beneath it is said never to fill with water. According to Wikipedia, the temple is believed to date from the 9th century and to be Paramara work, with the nearby fort renamed Achalgarh by Maharana Kumbha in 1452. Near the temple a four-tonne Nandi cast in panchadhatu, five metals, bears an inscription dated 1407; popular legend says the Nandi guards the temple from invaders, and that hidden bees have saved it on several occasions. Visitors also see quartz idols, a pond with three stone buffalo figures, and a large Champa tree. Maha Shivaratri is the principal festival.

description: Adhar Devi Temple, also called Arbuda Devi Temple, is a cave shrine in the hills just outside the town of Mount Abu, about 3 km from the main bus station. It is dedicated to Goddess Durga in her form as Arbuda Devi, the goddess associated with the Arbuda (Abu) hills. Reaching it involves climbing a flight of 365 steps cut into the rock. The sanctum sits inside a natural cleft, and devotees must stoop or crawl through a narrow passage to enter, with the interior lit by lamps. Local belief says the name 'Adhar' refers to the goddess's lip, which is said to have fallen here, and that her image appears suspended in mid-air. These accounts are traditional and no founding date or builder is given in the sources consulted. The temple is busiest during the nine days of Navratri. Nearby is Doodh Baori, a well regarded locally as sacred.

description: The Ajanta Caves are rock-cut Buddhist monuments carved into the wall of a horseshoe-shaped gorge of the Waghur river in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (formerly Aurangabad) district. The site has about thirty caves (originally numbered 1 to 29, with a few more identified later), a mix of viharas, or monasteries, and chaitya-grihas, or prayer halls. Wikipedia reports that work began in the 2nd century BCE and continued to about 480 CE, with an earlier phase linked to Satavahana-era patronage and a later Mahayana phase producing the most elaborate caves. Scholars disagree on the dates of the second phase; Walter Spink argues it mostly fell in 460 to 480 CE under the Vakataka king Harishena. The walls and ceilings carry paintings and sculpture that depict the Buddha and the Jataka tales of his past lives. A British officer, John Smith, drew wider attention to the caves in 1819, though local people already knew them. UNESCO inscribed Ajanta as a World Heritage Site in 1983, and the Archaeological Survey of India maintains it.

description: Mata no Madh is a village in Lakhpat taluka of Kutch district, about 105 km from Bhuj according to Wikipedia, and is the seat of the Ashapura Mata temple. The goddess is regarded as the family deity of the former Jadeja rulers of Kutch and is described on the Kachchh district administration's tourism page as the patron deity of Kachchh. According to Wikipedia, the temple was built in the 14th century by two Karad Vania men, Ajo and Anagor, and the 1819 earthquake damaged it and it was rebuilt in 1823; the 2001 earthquake caused further damage, which was later repaired. The main image is a red-painted stone figure about six feet high, reported to have come from Marwar. The shrine has a passage for walking around the deity. Large crowds gather during the Chaitra and Ashvin Navaratri festivals, with Ashvin considered the more important. A second Ashapura shrine on a nearby hill and a cave shrine at Jagora hill are also mentioned in the area.

description: Aundha Nagnath is a Shiva temple in the village of Aundha Nagnath in Hingoli district, in Maharashtra's Marathwada region. According to Wikipedia, the base, outer walls and sanctum belong to the Yadava period and use the Hemadpanti method of fitted stone without mortar, while the upper portion and spire were rebuilt later, probably in the 18th century. The sanctum lies below ground level and is reached by steps, and the Nandi pavilion stands behind the temple rather than in front. Wikipedia also states that the Archaeological Survey of India protects it as a monument of national importance. Devotees revere Nagnath as one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, a status also linked to the Nageshwar shrine in Gujarat. Local tradition credits the Pandavas with the first temple, and the renovation is commonly attributed to Ahilyabai Holkar. Festivals include Mahashivratri with a chariot procession, and Shravan Mondays, when pilgrims carry holy water on foot.

description: The Baroli (Badoli) temple complex lies near Rawatbhata in Chittorgarh district, close to the Chambal river and about 45 km southeast of Kota. It is a group of early medieval stone temples, usually dated to the 10th century and attributed to the Pratihara period, though some sources give the 10th to 11th centuries. Wikipedia counts eight temples within a walled enclosure and a ninth roughly a kilometre away, dedicated to forms of Shiva, Durga, Vishnu and Ganesha. The Ghateshwara Mahadeva temple is the largest and best preserved, with a finely carved tower, a lotus-patterned ceiling in the sanctum, a Nandi before the shrine and five lingas; its name is linked to one resembling an inverted pot. Other shrines are partly ruined. The Archaeological Survey of India lists eight of the temples as a monument of national significance. The complex is set among peepal, mango and jamun trees.

description: Bet Dwarka, also written Beyt Dwarka, is an inhabited island at the mouth of the Gulf of Kutch in Devbhumi Dwarka district, about 2 km across the water from Okha and roughly 25 km from Dwarka town. It is a Krishna pilgrimage centre. According to Wikipedia, the island's two main shrines are the Dwarkadhish Temple and the Shri Keshavraiji Temple, and its temples date from around the end of the 18th century. Gujarat Tourism credits the founding of the principal temple to Vallabhacharya and records the belief that Krishna stayed here, reading the name as 'bet', meaning gift. Another source describes Keshavraiji as the ishtdev (chosen deity) of the Pushkarna community. Wikipedia also notes that underwater and onshore finds point to settlement from the Late Harappan period onward. Pilgrims cross by ferry from Okha, and since February 2024 the Sudarshan Setu sea bridge has linked the island to the mainland.

description: Bhadrakali Temple stands within the Bhadra Fort precinct in the old walled city of Ahmedabad, in the Manek Chowk area. Its goddess, Bhadrakali, is honoured as a guardian of the city; Wikipedia describes the black four-armed image as a form of Lakshmi. Accounts of the temple's origin differ. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation's city website links it with King Karnadev of the Solanki dynasty, founder of Karnavati. Wikipedia instead says the shrine occupies a room in the north wing of the Azam Khan Sarai, built in 1637, and was converted during Maratha rule. Gujarat Tourism says Bhadra Fort, raised by Ahmad Shah I in 1411, took its name from the temple, while a plaque cited by Wikipedia ties the name to a Rajput citadel at Anhilwada-Patan. Navratri draws large numbers of visitors, with Garba and Raas. A newspaper reported that the temple trust organised a procession of the goddess's footprints on Ahmedabad's 614th foundation anniversary.

description: Bhadreshwar, in Mundra taluka of Kutch, is a Shvetambar Jain pilgrimage site, also called Vasai Jain Tirth. According to Wikipedia, the main shrine holds three white marble images: Ajitanatha, dated 1565 CE, flanked by Shantinatha and a seven-hooded Parshvanatha, both dated 1175 CE. The complex follows the plan of the Dilwara temples at Mount Abu, with a main shrine of about 15 by 26 metres ringed by 52 subsidiary shrines. Tradition recorded in the nineteenth-century Bantvijaya chronicles places its origins in 516 BCE, though Gujarat Tourism calls such early dates unreliable and unverified. Wikipedia reports that the merchant Jagdusha extensively renovated it in the thirteenth century. Earthquakes damaged it repeatedly, most severely in January 2001, after which it was rebuilt. The temple is administered by the Seth Vardhaman Kalyanji Trust.

description: Bhavnath Mahadev Temple stands at the foot of Mount Girnar on the edge of Junagadh, close to Girnar Taleti, where the climb up the hill begins, and near Damodar Kund. Shiva is worshipped here as Bhavnath, and local tradition holds that the linga appeared on its own. According to the account summarised on Wikipedia, a garment of Shiva and Parvati is said to have fallen at Mrigi Kund while they travelled over the Girnar hills, which is why the pond is held sacred. The temple is best known for the five-day Bhavnath fair, also called the Girnar Mahashivratri Mela, held in the month of Magha (February to March) and reaching its peak at midnight on Maha Shivratri. Naga sadhus of the Dashanami tradition arrive in procession, often on elephants, and bathe in Mrigi Kund before worship. In 2025 the Junagadh district administration took over management of the temple after the tenure of its mahant ended.

description: Birla Mandir, also known as the Lakshmi Narayan Temple, stands on raised ground at the foot of Moti Dungri hill in the Tilak Nagar area of Jaipur. It is dedicated to Vishnu as Narayan and his consort Lakshmi, with a shrine to Ganesha also noted. The B. M. Birla Foundation built it, and it was completed in 1988. It is built entirely of white marble in a modern style, topped by three domes, and the images of Lakshmi and Narayan are described as carved from a single block. The temple is set within gardens and is lit up in the evening, which makes it a prominent landmark below the hill.

description: Dwarkadhish Temple stands on the southern bank of Rajsamand Lake at Kankroli, Rajsamand district. It belongs to the Pushtimarg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya, and its presiding deity, Krishna as Dwarkadhish, is counted among the tradition's seven swaroops. Accounts say the image was originally at Gokul and was moved to Ahmedabad in the Mughal period before being brought to Mewar and installed first at the village of Asotiya. After Rajsamand Lake was built, that shrine was flooded, and higher ground was granted for the present temple. Sources disagree on dates: Wikipedia gives 1671 for the invitation to Mewar and 1676 as the completion year, while a heritage-portal account gives 1726 for installation at Asotiya and about 1776 for the new site. The haveli-style building overlooks the lake. Festival days noted by a heritage portal include Poonam (full moon) days, Holi, Diwali, Ram Navami, Janmashtami and Akshaya Tritiya.

description: Eklingji is a Shiva temple complex at Kailashpuri in Girwa tehsil, Udaipur district, about 20 km north of Udaipur city and near Nagda, the former capital of Mewar. The deity is regarded as the kuladevata of Mewar's ruling house, and the Maharanas are traditionally described as acting on the god's behalf as his regent or dewan. The form is often described as Harihara. The 15th-century Ekalinga Mahatmya credits Bappa Rawal with building the first temple in the 8th century, which Live History India calls a legend. Wikipedia says that temple was destroyed during sultanate invasions and the shrine was rebuilt several times. Sources mention renovation by Hamir, Mokal and Rana Kumbha, and the last major rebuilding under Rana Raimal (reigned 1473 to 1509). Live History India associates his reign with the present black marble image, whose four faces are explained as Brahma, Vishnu, Surya and Rudra. Wikipedia notes the site likely began under the Pashupata sect. It is described as a private shrine of the Mewar family, though the public may pray there.

description: Shri Gajanan Maharaj Sansthan in Shegaon, Buldhana district, Maharashtra, is the trust that looks after the samadhi temple of the saint Gajanan Maharaj. description: Ganpatipule is a small coastal village on the Konkan shore of Ratnagiri district, roughly 25 to 30 km from Ratnagiri town. Its temple is dedicated to Ganesha, worshipped here as a swayambhu, or self-manifested, image that faces west toward the Arabian Sea; the temple trust describes him as the Western Sentinel deity and counts the site among the Ashta Dwar Devata. According to local tradition, a Brahmin named Balbhatji Bhide, who rented the village, fasted and worshipped in the forest and was shown the image in a vision; a cowherd then saw a cow's milk flowing over the spot, and clearing it revealed the idol. Wikipedia describes the idol as about 400 years old and records a folk explanation of the name Ganpatipule. The trust's own history page dates the shrine to the Peshwa era. Magh Chaturthi and Gauri Ganpati are among the major festivals, and the beach beside the temple is part of the visit.

description: Govind Dev Ji Temple lies within the City Palace complex in Jaipur and is dedicated to Krishna as Govind Dev, together with Radha. According to Wikipedia, the image is counted among the seven principal Goswami deities of Vrindavan, and tradition holds that it was made by Bajranabh, Krishna's great-grandson. Rupa Goswami is said to have rediscovered it and built a temple in Vrindavan around 1535. After Vrindavan was attacked in 1670 the icons were moved, first to Kaman, and the journey to Jaipur took many years. A popular account says the deity appeared to the king in a dream and asked to be brought to Jaipur. The temple has a large Satsang Hall with a 119-foot single-span concrete roof. Crowds gather especially at Janmashtami.

description: Jagdish Temple stands in the old city of Udaipur, a short walk from the City Palace. Four smaller shrines around the main one are dedicated to Ganesha, Surya, Shakti and Shiva. It remains an active centre of Vaishnava worship in the heart of Udaipur.

description: Kayavarohan, also called Karvan, is a village in Vadodara district about 30 km from Vadodara city. description: Kopeshwar Temple is a Shiva temple in Khidrapur village on the Krishna river, in Kolhapur district, Maharashtra, about 60 km east of Kolhapur city. The plan has four parts: the open-roofed Swargamandapa with 48 carved pillars, a sabha mandapa, an antechamber and the sanctum. Unusually for a Shiva temple, a Vishnu image known as Dhopeshwar is described alongside the Kopeshwar linga, and there is no Nandi shrine; a local legend connects this to Shiva and Daksha. Many sculptures are damaged, and, according to Live History India, the site is under the care of the Archaeological Survey of India.

description: Narayan Sarovar is a pilgrimage village on Kori Creek in Lakhpat taluka of Kutch, in far western Gujarat. description: Ramtek Gad Mandir is a group of temples on a hill above the town of Ramtek, about 50 km from Nagpur in Nagpur district. Tradition also holds that the poet Kalidasa composed the Meghaduta in these hills. Ram Navami and Kartik Utsav are among the major occasions observed here.

description: Rani Sati Temple is in Jhunjhunu town, the headquarters of Jhunjhunu district in Rajasthan's Shekhawati region. The temple is dedicated to Rani Sati, also called Narayani Devi or Dadiji. In the legend, a young bride's husband is killed and she dies on his funeral pyre; other versions say she died resisting capture. Accounts of her life vary widely, and sources place her death anywhere from the 13th to the 17th century. Tradition links her to Uttara of the Mahabharata, and devotees regard her as a manifestation of Shakti or Durga. According to Wikipedia, the shrine began in 1912 as simple memorial mounds, and a larger complex was built between 1917 and 1936 with funds from the Jalan family of the Agarwal community. The marble complex has no statue of the goddess; a trident is worshipped and a portrait hangs in the main hall. The grounds also include shrines to Hanuman, Ganesha and Shiva and twelve smaller sati shrines. Sati practice and its glorification are prohibited under Indian law (the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987). According to Wikipedia, after the 1987 Deorala case the courts allowed worship of Rani Sati inside the temple but did not permit ceremonies celebrating the sati or the annual fair on the outer grounds.

description: Trinetra Ganesh Temple sits inside Ranthambore Fort, within Ranthambore National Park near Sawai Madhopur in eastern Rajasthan. The deity is a three-eyed form of Ganesha, revered as the first god invoked before new undertakings. According to Wikipedia, local belief places the shrine's origin at more than 700 years ago: while besieged by Alauddin Khilji's army around 1299-1301, the Chauhan ruler Hammir is said to have dreamed of Ganesha and then raised the temple at a self-manifested image. The fort is part of the UNESCO-listed Hill Forts of Rajasthan, and visitors enter through the protected tiger reserve area.

description: Rudra Mahalaya, also called Rudramal, is the ruined remains of a large Shaiva temple complex in Siddhpur, Patan district. According to Wikipedia, construction began in 943 CE under the Chaulukya ruler Mularaja and the complex was completed and consecrated in 1140 CE by Jayasimha Siddharaja. It is described as a sandstone structure in the Maru-Gurjara style. The complex was damaged during a Delhi Sultanate raid in the late 1290s, attributed to Alauddin Khalji's forces, and later in the early fifteenth century Ahmad Shah I of Gujarat demolished much of it and reused its western portion as a congregational mosque. What survives today is limited, chiefly two ornamental gateways (torans) and a few pillars of the central structure (a Wikipedia claim awaiting citation). The site is listed by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance, under number N-GJ-164.

description: Sas Bahu Temples are a pair of Hindu temples at Nagda village in Girwa tehsil, Udaipur district, close to Eklingji. The larger shrine is called Sas and the smaller Bahu, words meaning mother-in-law and daughter-in-law in present usage; the original name is given as Sahasrabahu, "thousand-armed", an epithet of Vishnu. The Archaeological Survey of India describes the complex as a twin Vaishnava group and, on stylistic grounds, assigns the intact north-east shrine to the last quarter of the tenth century, while Wikipedia notes that a 2018 ASI board gives the early eleventh century. The outer walls are mostly plain, but the interiors carry relief carving including Ramayana scenes, and corner images show Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu. The site is a protected monument and has no entry fee.

description: Shrinathji Temple in Nathdwara, in Rajsamand district, is a major Vaishnava pilgrimage centre of the Pushtimarg tradition and is managed by the Nathdwara Temple Board, set up under the Nathdwara Temple Act of 1959.
